latin: Anima quae peccauit uel in terreno uel in aereo corpore post mortem bruti uitam uiuit.
translation: The soul that has sinned, whether in an earthly or an aerial body, lives the life of a brute after death.
translation_note: The thesis states a doctrine of metempsychosis into non-rational animal life as punishment for sin, attributed to Plotinus; 'aereo corpore' reflects the Neoplatonic notion of an intermediate, aerial vehicle of the soul distinct from its earthly body (farmer1998:15094).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch8, from Latin at farmer1998:15094

sources.text: Pico's own thesis 5>51, which Farmer glosses as opposing Plotinus, arguing from a saying of Plato in the Phaedrus
sources.pico_relation: Farmer's note explicitly cross-references this thesis as 'opposing Plotinus'

sources.text: the belief in transcorporation of souls among all the wise men of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians and Chaldeans, in Pico's own thesis 21.8
sources.pico_relation: Farmer's note groups this thesis with 21.8 under the same topic of transmigration

doctrine: The thesis holds that a soul which has sinned, whether in an earthly or an aerial body, lives the life of a brute animal after death (farmer1998:15094). Farmer's note cross-references three other theses on the same topic of the transmigration of souls: 21.8, attributed to 'Adeland the Arab,' which states that all the wise men of the Indians, Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans believed in the transcorporation of souls (farmer1998:15366); Pico's own thesis 5>51, which Farmer glosses as opposing Plotinus, arguing from a saying of Plato in the Phaedrus that, rightly understood, it shows Plotinus's position positing the transmigration of souls into brutes to be mistaken (farmer1998:23083); and 8>4, on transanimation into plant life, which Farmer connects to a similar view in Empedocles (farmer1998:24832). Farmer's note also cites Plotinus's Enneads 1.1.11 and following as the classical source (farmer1998:15126).
context: Howlett reports Ogren's argument that, on this point of Kabbalistic-Platonic doctrine, Pico 'leans more on Plotinus, Ficino on Kabbalism,' citing this thesis's Latin (howlett2021:9186).
historiography: Howlett's footnotes are the only scholarship on this thesis in the material opened; besides reporting Ogren's argument, she notes that Copenhaver 'notes that the transmigration of souls was...', a sentence cut off in the material consulted (howlett2021:9186).

quotations.text: Pico leans more on Plotinus, Ficino on Kabbalism

not_established: The content of Copenhaver's note on the transmigration of souls, referenced by Howlett but cut off in the material consulted, is not established by the sources consulted.
The specific argument in Ogren (2009a) beyond Howlett's summary is not established, since Ogren's own text was not opened.
